From Words to Worlds:
Image Captioning with a CLIP Encoder
and a GPT-2 Decoder

Milestone 3 — Evaluation and Analysis
IE 7615 Deep Learning for AI
Generative Project

Team members: Zhiming Hu, Wan Luo
November 25, 2026

Code repository: github.com/DeepLearningNEU/GP1
Evaluation notebook: notebooks/03_evaluation.ipynb

1. Methods

1.1 Model

The captioner encodes each image with the CLIP ViT-L/14 vision Transformer, which stays frozen; its features are pre-computed once. GPT-2 small (124M) generates the caption. Captions are fed to GPT-2 as <|endoftext|> caption <|endoftext|>, and the loss is the cross-entropy on the caption tokens and the end token. The image reaches the decoder through one of two embedding-injection methods:

  • Prefix conditioning (ClipCap-style): a 2-layer MLP maps the 768-d CLIP image embedding to 10 vectors in GPT-2's input space, which are prepended to the caption tokens. GPT-2 attends to them through its ordinary causal self-attention.
  • Cross-attention: the 257 CLIP patch tokens (1024-d) are projected to 768-d. Every GPT-2 block gets a new cross-attention layer that attends from the caption tokens to these patches.

1.2 Fine-tuning strategies

For each injection method we compare three ways of training the pre-trained GPT-2 weights. The new image layers (the MLP mapper, or the projection plus the cross-attention layers) are always trained.

StrategyWhat is trained
Full fine-tuningall GPT-2 weights (learning rate 5e-5) and the new image layers (2e-4)
LoRAGPT-2 frozen; rank-8 LoRA adapters (alpha = 16, dropout 0.05) on every self-attention c_attn / c_proj, learning rate 0.0002; plus the new image layers
Prefix tuning (frozen GPT-2)GPT-2 completely frozen; only the new image layers. With prefix injection, the image-conditioned prefix is the only thing learned (prefix tuning)

1.3 Data and training protocol

  • Training set: 5,000 COCO train2017 images with all of their captions (25,007 image–caption pairs).
  • Model-selection set: COCO val2017 images 1,001–5,000. After every epoch we compute the validation loss on these images and keep the checkpoint with the lowest loss. This early stopping fixes the overfitting we observed in Milestone 2.
  • Test set: the first 1,000 val2017 images, each with 5 human reference captions. These images are not used for training or model selection, and every number in Section 2 is computed on them.
  • Optimization: AdamW, batch 32, 300 warm-up steps then linear decay, gradient clipping 1.0, at most 5 epochs. All 6 models were trained on NEU Explorer HPC GPUs: the prefix models on a Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB, the cross-attention models on a Tesla P100-PCIE-12GB.

1.4 Decoding strategies

  • Greedy: take the most likely token at each step.
  • Beam search: keep the K best hypotheses, K ∈ {2, 3, 5, 8, 10}, with length-normalized scores.
  • Temperature sampling: sample from softmax(logits / T) with T ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5}.
  • Nucleus (top-p) sampling: p ∈ {0.5, 0.9} at T = 1.

All decoding settings were run with the two fully fine-tuned models; the LoRA and prefix-tuning models were decoded with greedy, beam-3 and nucleus p = 0.9. Sampling uses a fixed random seed, and generation stops at the end token or after 30 tokens.

1.5 Metrics

  • BLEU-1..4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr (pycocoevalcap). Each generated caption is compared with its 5 references after lower-casing and removing punctuation.
    • BLEU measures n-gram precision.
    • METEOR matches words, including stems and synonyms, and balances recall against precision.
    • ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence.
    • CIDEr is a consensus metric: TF-IDF-weighted n-gram similarity, so words that are informative across the dataset count more.
  • Image–caption alignment: CLIPScore = 2.5 · max(cos(CLIP image, CLIP caption), 0), computed with CLIP ViT-L/14. It needs no references, so it measures whether the caption describes the image. We also inspect captions by hand, including the highest- and lowest-scoring ones.
  • Diversity: distinct-2, the number of unique bigrams divided by all bigrams across the 1,000 captions; and the share of captions that are unique.

Figure 1. Validation loss on the model-selection images after each epoch.

Full fine-tuning gives the lowest validation loss for both injection methods, but it overfits after epoch 2–3. Its validation loss rises by epoch 5 to 2.27 (prefix) and 2.45 (cross-attention). Early stopping keeps the epoch-3 and epoch-2 checkpoints. LoRA and prefix tuning keep GPT-2 frozen, so they overfit much less. Prefix tuning with prefix injection still improves at epoch 5 (2.50), so it is under-trained after 5 epochs. Training times are not comparable across the two injection methods: the prefix models ran on a V100, the cross-attention models on a P100.

Table 2. Test-set results with beam search (width 3). Bold marks the best value in each column.
Figure 2. CIDEr, METEOR and CLIPScore by fine-tuning strategy and injection method (beam-3, 1,000 test images).

Cross-attention: freezing GPT-2 does not hurt, and it gives the best test CIDEr of all six models (1.103, against 1.075 for full fine-tuning and 1.073 for LoRA). It trains only 19% as many parameters (29.2M vs 153.6M). The three strategies tie on METEOR (0.267–0.268). Full fine-tuning keeps a small edge on BLEU-4 (0.334 vs 0.331 frozen and 0.313 LoRA). The new cross-attention layers already give the model enough capacity to read the image, so updating GPT-2 itself adds little. On only 5,000 training images, keeping GPT-2 frozen also acts as a regularizer. Lower validation loss does not mean better captions: full fine-tuning has the lowest validation loss (2.229) but not the best CIDEr.

Prefix conditioning: LoRA matches full fine-tuning (CIDEr 1.001 vs 0.992, METEOR 0.251 vs 0.255). It needs only 0.44M adapter weights on top of the mapper, i.e. 32.9M trainable parameters instead of 156.9M. Pure prefix tuning is clearly weaker (CIDEr 0.925, METEOR 0.239, BLEU-4 0.272). Ten prefix vectors are the only way to steer a frozen GPT-2, which is harder to learn, and its validation loss was still falling after 5 epochs. More epochs would likely close part of the gap.

Image alignment: CLIPScore is almost the same for all six models (0.594–0.607). The strategies differ mainly in how closely the wording matches the human references, not in whether the caption describes the image.

2.3 Parameter sensitivity

Beam width.

Figure 3. Effect of beam width (1 = greedy) for the two fully fine-tuned models.

Going from greedy decoding to beam search with width 3 raises CIDEr by 0.068 (cross-attention) and 0.046 (prefix), and METEOR by about 0.01. Beyond width 3–5 the gains stop: CIDEr peaks at width 5 for cross-attention (1.088) and at width 8 for prefix (1.008), and changes by less than 0.01 afterwards. Wider beams cost diversity and speed. Distinct-2 falls steadily (cross-attention: 0.183 at width 1 to 0.146 at width 10), the share of unique captions drops from 89% to 81%, and decoding time grows about 8× from greedy to width 10. CLIPScore also drifts down slightly (0.604 to 0.597). Width 3–5 is the best trade-off.

Temperature.

Figure 4. Effect of the sampling temperature (pure sampling, top-p = 1).

Temperature trades accuracy for diversity, and every step moves both in the same direction. At T = 0.25, sampling is close to greedy (CIDEr 0.982 vs 1.007, cross-attention). At T = 1.0, CIDEr halves (0.50), and at T = 1.5 the captions are almost unrelated to the references (CIDEr 0.07). Diversity rises over the same range: distinct-2 goes from 0.20 to 0.91, every caption is unique from T = 1.0 on, and the average length grows from 9.8 to 14.5 words because the model rambles. CLIPScore drops from 0.60 to 0.41 (Figure 4), so high temperatures make captions drift away from the image, not only from the reference wording. The two injection methods behave almost the same once T ≥ 1.25: sampling noise then outweighs the difference in how the image is injected.

Injection method. With full fine-tuning, cross-attention beats prefix conditioning for every deterministic decoding setting: CIDEr is 1.075 vs 0.992 with beam-3 and 1.007 vs 0.946 with greedy, and METEOR is about 0.012 higher. With frozen GPT-2 the gap is largest (1.103 vs 0.925). Cross-attention reads all 257 patch tokens at every decoding step instead of one pooled vector, which helps it name objects and their relations. Prefix conditioning produces slightly more varied text (distinct-2 0.206 vs 0.183 with greedy) but less accurate text. The decoding times in the tables are only comparable within one injection method, because the two were evaluated on different GPUs (V100 for prefix, P100 for cross-attention).

Table 4. Every decoding setting, cross-attention (full fine-tuning).

Figure 5 shows a single accuracy–diversity frontier shared by both models.

  • Beam search sits in the high-accuracy, low-diversity corner.
  • Greedy is close to beam search but slightly more diverse.
  • Sampling trades accuracy for diversity as the temperature rises.
  • Nucleus sampling sits on the same curve. Truncating the tail makes p = 0.9 more accurate than pure sampling at the same temperature (CIDEr 0.60 vs 0.50 at T = 1), and p = 0.5 behaves like T = 0.5.
For a single accurate caption, use beam search with width 3–5. When several different captions per image are wanted, nucleus p = 0.5 or T = 0.5 is the best compromise: it keeps about 83% of the beam-3 CIDEr with about 1.55× its distinct-2 (cross-attention).

Figure 6. Per-image CIDEr against CLIPScore (beam-3).

For all eight random images the best model names the main scene and objects correctly: a crew in a boat, a stop sign, horses in a field, kitchens, zebras, a bus, and a woman with sheep.

  • Repetition: "A stop sign with a stop sign in front of it." The caption also misses the blue street sign.
  • Wrong attributes: the mostly white bus with red trim becomes "a red bus".
  • Details that are not in the image: these mostly come from nucleus sampling, e.g. "a zebra eating from a dirt, dirty branch" and "a person standing on a hillside eating hay from a fence".
The two top-scoring captions are specific and correct (a couple eating doughnuts, a man holding a Wii remote). The third shows that CLIPScore can be fooled: the image is a statue holding a kite, but "a person flying a kite" still scores 0.85. The lowest-CLIPScore caption is a real failure: three carved jack-o'-lanterns are described as "a group of friends holding up a rainbow flag" (CLIPScore 0.13, CIDEr 0.02). None of the captions of our 5,000 training images mentions a pumpkin or jack-o'-lantern, so the model has never seen the object named.

The per-image correlation between CLIPScore and CIDEr is only r = 0.34 (Figure 6), so the two metrics measure different things. CIDEr penalizes correct captions that are worded differently from the references, while CLIPScore checks the image–text match but ignores fluency and small details. We therefore report both, alongside the n-gram metrics.

2.6 Summary of findings

  1. Best model: cross-attention with frozen GPT-2 and beam-3 decoding. On the 1,000 held-out test images it reaches CIDEr 1.103, BLEU-4 0.331, METEOR 0.268 and ROUGE-L 0.557, while training only 29.2M parameters.
  2. Injection method: cross-attention beats prefix conditioning under every fine-tuning strategy and every deterministic decoding setting. The gap is largest when GPT-2 is frozen.
  3. Fine-tuning: parameter-efficient training is enough. LoRA matches full fine-tuning for prefix conditioning, and frozen GPT-2 matches or beats it for cross-attention. Full fine-tuning overfits our 5,000-image training set after 2–3 epochs. Pure prefix tuning, with a frozen GPT-2 steered only by the prefix, needs more training than 5 epochs.
  4. Decoding: beam width helps up to 3–5 and then only costs time and diversity. Temperature trades accuracy for diversity and also lowers image alignment (CLIPScore 0.60 to 0.41). Nucleus truncation improves on pure sampling.
  5. Metrics: reference-based and reference-free metrics agree only weakly (r = 0.34), so we report both.
